source: FAO Regional Office for Asia and the Pacific, Swine Health Management, Volume 2: Guide to Prevent and Control Porcine Reproductive and Respiratory Syndrome (RAP Publication 2012/27, Bangkok, 2012)
text: The main source of PRRS virus is an infected pig. Other pigs can catch it through direct contact — especially nose-to-nose contact — with the sick pig's mucus, saliva, urine, milk, or feces. The virus also spreads through: infected boar semen (infectious for up to 43 days after the boar is infected); contaminated vehicles and trading of pigs, especially when sick animals are sold before disease is suspected to be confirmed; people and shared equipment moving between farms; needles reused between pigs; houseflies and mosquitoes, which can carry the virus up to 2 km; chickens and ducks, which can shed the virus in their droppings; and airborne spread over short distances during cool, humid, low-wind conditions — farms should ideally be at least 1.5 km apart. Raw or undercooked pig meat (swill) fed to pigs can also transmit the virus if it comes from a sick animal.
